t: Minimize the Maximum Edge Weight of Graph — Threshold Reachability
o: Delete edges so every node can reach node 0, minimizing the maximum kept edge weight, subject to at most threshold outgoing edges per node. Binary search on the weight bound W: keeping only edges of weight <= W, every node must reach 0. Crucially, the degree constraint is never binding — if all nodes reach 0 in the <= W subgraph, a single inbound tree toward 0 (one outgoing edge per node) suffices, and threshold >= 1 always permits it. Example 3: with W = 2 the edges 1->2, 2->3, 4->0 connect everyone; W = 1 fails.
k: Feasibility for a bound W is pure reachability: every node reaches 0 using only edges of weight <= W.
The threshold constraint is automatically satisfiable via a spanning in-tree to node 0, so it can be ignored beyond checking threshold >= 1 (guaranteed).

a.i: Binary search the answer over edge weights. For a candidate W, build the reverse graph (edge a->b becomes b->a) restricted to weight <= W and BFS/DFS from node 0; feasible iff all n nodes are visited. Monotonicity (larger W keeps more edges) makes the predicate binary-searchable.
s: Predicate ok(W): reverse adjacency with w <= W; BFS from 0; return visited count == n.
Binary search the smallest feasible W in [1, maxWeight].
a.t: O(E log W) — O(log(maxWeight)) binary-search rounds, each an O(n + E) BFS.
a.sp: O(n + E) — the filtered reverse graph and visited array.

a.i: Equivalent to Kruskal: process edges in increasing weight, unioning a->b as an undirected connection (reachability to 0 is undirected connectivity in the reversed sense). The answer is the weight of the edge whose addition makes every node lie in node 0's component; if that never happens, return -1. One sort plus one pass, no binary search.
s: Union-find over nodes; for each edge (a, b, w) in order, union(a, b).
After each union, if all nodes share 0's root, return w.
If the loop finishes without full connectivity, return -1.
a.t: O(E log E + n*E) — sorting dominates; the naive all-nodes check per edge can be made O(E α(n)) with a component-size counter.
a.sp: O(n + E) — union-find array and the sorted edge list.

w: Binary search + BFS is the most explainable; DSU is faster to code and elegantly avoids the search. The key interview insight to state explicitly: threshold >= 1 makes the degree constraint redundant because a single in-tree to node 0 satisfies it. Pitfalls: direction of edges in the reachability check (reverse them — we need 'everything reaches 0', not '0 reaches everything'), and returning -1 when even the full graph fails. Follow-up: if threshold could be 0, only node 0 itself is feasible; if edges were undirected, the problem becomes a bottleneck-spanning-tree question solvable identically.
